tagline: Where Spain's royal road ran into French Louisiana.
intro: The spine of the byway is LA 6, from the Texas line through Many to Natchitoches, roughly on the line of El Camino Real de los Tejas, the Spanish road that came up from Mexico and ended there. The old trail crossed the Sabine on a ferry that ran from about 1795 until a bridge took over in 1937. From Clarence, US 84 carries on east across central Louisiana to the Mississippi at Vidalia, across from Natchez.

Other highways belong to it too, out to Jena, Marksville and Sicily Island, so the byway is more a web than a road. Its western end was long disputed ground, first between France and Spain and then between Spain and the United States.

moments.title: Fort Jesup
moments.text: Zachary Taylor set up this post in 1822 to bring order to the Neutral Strip, the land between the Sabine and the Arroyo Hondo that both nations had agreed to leave alone.

moments.title: Los Adaes
moments.text: For half a century the capital of Spanish Texas stood here on what is now the Louisiana side, a presidio and mission set down to keep watch on the French at Natchitoches.

moments.title: Natchitoches
moments.text: The oldest permanent settlement in the Louisiana Purchase, founded by the French in 1714, keeps Front Street paved in brick, lately relaid one numbered brick at a time.
